html:
Around 2200 BCE farmers and seafarers from Taiwan crossed to the Batanes Islands and northern Luzon in the Philippines. It was the first step out of Taiwan in the Austronesian expansion, which in the end reached from Madagascar to Easter Island.

These people spoke early Austronesian languages, grew rice and millet, kept pigs and dogs, and made red-slipped pottery. Their sailing technology was the key: outrigger canoes, catamarans and sails, in use some time before 2000 BCE. Along the way they met and mixed with the older hunter-gatherer peoples of the islands, whose ancestors had arrived tens of thousands of years earlier.

From the Philippines the expansion branched out:

  • South and west into Borneo, Sulawesi, Java and Sumatra, and onto the coasts of mainland Southeast Asia, where the Cham are their descendants.
  • East to the Mariana Islands and into Island Melanesia, where the Lapita voyagers appear around 1600 BCE.
  • Much later, across the Indian Ocean in the settlement of Madagascar.
  • Across Polynesia in the settlement of East Polynesia, ending in New Zealand around 1250 to 1300.

Today about 400 million people speak Austronesian languages, among them Filipino, Malay, Indonesian, Malagasy, Hawaiian and Māori. Their shared words for canoe, sail and outrigger still show where they came from.
